When a Friend Tells You Something Scary

Upper School · Counselor-led small group, 25 minutes (one-on-one version below) · Any grade

Before you start

Each slide carries its own point, so you can talk with the room instead of reading notes. Tell them up front what you’d have to act on if something comes up in the room. Be ready to explain plainly what you’d share and with whom, and invite students to tell you how they’re doing, too.

Every student in the room

On the what-happens-after slide, name that some families keep problems inside or fear agencies, including families with immigration worries, and that a counselor plans around that.

Slide 1 · Notes

Keep it light for ten seconds, then go straight to the next slide.

Slide 2 · Notes

Tell them up front what you’d have to act on if something comes up in the room. Anyone can step out.

Slide 3 · Notes

Evans, Hawton and Rodham: 6,020 students aged 15 and 16. Ask: “What makes a friend the first person someone tells?” Trust, they won’t freak out, they won’t tell parents. “That trust is exactly why your next move matters.”

Slide 4 · Notes

The answer. Let the room react before you move on.

Slide 5 · Notes

About 1 in 4 survivors of a nearly fatal attempt said under five minutes passed between deciding and acting (Simon et al., 2001), which is why Now can’t wait until morning. Help get pills, weapons or anything they might use out of reach. Quick sort: read three one-line examples; students hold up 1, 2 or 3 fingers.

Slide 6 · Notes

Explain what you actually do: listen, check how safe the friend is, make a plan, involve family when that’s safe. If the danger is an adult at home, staff must report it, so the student isn’t the one who has to fix it. Some families fear agencies, including families with immigration worries; a counselor plans around that.

Slide 7 · Notes

Gould et al. (2005). The most at-risk students seemed less distressed after being asked.

Slide 8 · Notes

The answer. Let the room react before you move on.

Slide 9 · Notes

Then: stay their friend. Text, sit at lunch, act normal. Sources of Strength: trained peer leaders were about four times more likely to connect a suicidal friend with an adult (Wyman et al., 2010). If the friend refuses, the student still tells.

Slide 10 · Notes

Pairs. Each student says the direct question out loud to their partner, in their own words. It’s awkward; that’s the point of practicing.

Slide 11 · Notes

Take a few. Then three hard calls, one at a time.

Slide 12 · Notes

Today level. Not confronting the stepdad. Staff report it, so Will isn’t the one who has to fix it.

Slide 13 · Notes

The answer. Let the room react before you move on.

Slide 14 · Notes

Today level. Eating problems happen to every gender.

Slide 15 · Notes

The answer. Let the room react before you move on.

This is the hardest card. Ask what makes a DM feel like enough, and why it isn’t.

Slide 17 · Notes

The answer. Let the room react before you move on.

Slide 18 · Notes

Replaying it, bad sleep, guilt, anger at the friend for putting you there: all normal, none of it means you did something wrong. Invite them to tell you how they’re doing, not only how the friend is.

If you want more

The full plan, care notes, and research. None of it is needed to teach the lesson.

Lesson plan

A suggested plan. Change the timing, skip or reorder slides, or use any part on its own. You know your students.

Goal

Students learn how to sort what a friend tells them by urgency, practice the direct suicide question and the first five minutes, know which adult to reach at any hour, and recognize that hearing a disclosure can weigh on them too.

Materials

  • The deck on the big screen. Each slide carries its own point, so no script is needed.
  • Index cards, one per student
  • Pens
  • The take-home link to share afterward

Flow

  1. 3 minBefore we start, and who they tell first
  2. 4 minHow urgent is it? Now, today, this week
  3. 3 minWhy it’s hard, and the asking guess
  4. 5 minThe first five minutes, and say it out loud
  5. 2 minShare out
  6. 5 minThree hard calls: Will, Kate, Adam
  7. 3 minCarrying it, close

One on one (about 15 minutes)

One on one, often after a student has heard something: what they heard and how urgent it is (4). What happens after they tell, including what you'd have to share and whether their name comes up (4). How they're doing with it (4). Who they'd call after 9 p.m. next time (3).

Before you teach
Often a follow-up.

This group fits students who've recently heard something hard, or a peer-support group. A student currently holding a disclosure may need an individual conversation first.

Explain your own role plainly.

Students hold back because they don't know what happens next. Tell them what you do after a student comes to you, what you'd have to report, and when their name does or doesn't come up.

Practice the words out loud.

The direct question is hard to say the first time. Have each student say it to a partner. It lands very differently than reading it.

No real names.

Remind the group not to use real names or identifying details. If someone starts describing a real situation, move it to an individual conversation.

The listener carries it too.

Students who've received disclosures often feel guilt, anger at the friend, or trouble sleeping. Give that its own time at the end.

Adam's card is the hardest.

Students tend to choose the DM. Name that a post at 12:40 a.m. that sounds like a goodbye means waking an adult and calling 988, even when the person jokes like this often.

Every student in the room

Culture, family, identity, ability and money: what to keep in mind for this topic.

Families handle hard things differently.

In some families problems stay inside, mental health isn't discussed, or contact with any agency is frightening. Students should know that telling a counselor about this changes how the counselor helps.

Immigration and police.

Fear of police or immigration consequences keeps some students silent. Name mobile crisis and 988 as options that usually don't involve police, and be honest that 911 is for immediate danger.

Every gender and relationship.

The partner-control example can involve any genders. Make sure students hear that boys and LGBTQ+ teens can be on either side of a controlling relationship.

LGBTQ+ friends.

A friend who came out may also be the one at risk at home. Name that outing someone is never the adult step; going to a counselor is.

Different hours, different adults.

Not every student has a parent they can wake at 1 a.m. Build the who-to-call list with relatives, a friend's parent, faith leaders and 988.

Language.

Many crisis lines offer interpretation. If a friend's family doesn't speak English at home, name that as a solvable problem, not a reason to wait.

What the research says

In 6,020 students aged 15 and 16, teens who had self-harmed or thought about it were more likely to go to a friend than anyone else, and many who felt they needed help never asked anyone.

Evans, Hawton and Rodham, Journal of Adolescence, 2005

Among people aged 13 to 34 who survived a nearly fatal attempt, about 1 in 4 said less than five minutes passed between deciding and acting.

Simon et al., Suicide and Life-Threatening Behavior, 2001

In 2,342 New York high school students randomly assigned to be asked about suicide or not, those asked were no more distressed or suicidal, including the students at highest risk.

Gould et al., JAMA, 2005

Reviews keep finding that asking about suicide doesn't raise suicidal thinking.

Dazzi et al., Psychological Medicine, 2014

In a randomized trial in 18 high schools, trained peer leaders were about four times more likely than untrained peers to connect a suicidal friend with an adult.

Wyman et al. (Sources of Strength), American Journal of Public Health, 2010
